```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
                     out.width = "100%")
```

When does a zebra travel, forage or rest? We use the GPS track of one plains
zebra in Hwange National Park, Zimbabwe, and the rules proposed by
[Bouderbala, Nicosia and Fortin (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0360547).
The package includes 6,377 observed steps, each 30 minutes long. Gaps separate
the track into 28 segments.

## Fit the models

The prepared data give each step's length and turning angle, along with the
direction to the nearest grassland cell from the start of the step. This
makes the target available before the zebra moves.

```{r fit}
library(behavSSF)

zebra <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hwange-zebra-steps.rds",
                            package = "behavSSF"))
steps <- prepare_ssf_steps(zebra, density_measure = "area",
                           time = "time", expected_interval = 1800)

result <- fit_guided_ssf(
  steps, convention = "area", target = "cos_diff_theta_to_target",
  normalization = "exact", n_starts = 8, short_iter = 100, long_iter = 900,
  seed = 1729
)
result
```

With the default taxonomy, the function first tries habitat-directed
travelling (HDT), foraging and resting. The travelling state must have
the longest mean step and more concentrated turns than the foraging state.
For the HDT label, the 95% confidence interval for the travelling state's
grassland coefficient must lie above zero. If that model fails its checks,
the function tries travelling, foraging and resting without a grassland
term, then travelling and encamped, and finally a single state. It stops
at the first model that passes.

## Read the labels

The article reported habitat-directed travelling, foraging and resting.
Its archived code chose the nearest grassland cell using the observed
step endpoint. Here the cell is chosen at the start of the step, and
the likelihood is integrated directly. In this fit the travelling state's
grassland interval includes zero, so the package selects travelling,
foraging and resting.

```{r step-labels}
overview <- summary(result)
states <- overview$states
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  State = states$state,
  Steps = states$n_steps,
  `Mean step (m)` = round(1000 * states$mean_step),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

The counts come from the Viterbi sequence, which assigns one label to each
step. The means come from the fitted movement distributions.
`overview$candidates` gives the outcome of each candidate that was tried.

## See the states on the track

This map shows the first 48 hours of the longest segment. The open circle
marks where the excerpt starts.

```{r track, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8, fig.alt="Map of 48 hours of the Hwange zebra track coloured by inferred state. An open circle marks the start."}
library(ggplot2)

longest <- names(which.max(table(zebra$ID)))
plot(result, type = "track", segment = longest, step_range = c(1, 96)) +
  labs(title = "48 hours on the zebra's track",
       x = "Relative easting (km)", y = "Relative northing (km)")
```

The probability plot shows how strongly the fitted model supports each state.
When two curves are close, the model gives similar support to the two labels
at that step.

```{r posterior, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Smoothed probabilities of travelling, foraging and resting over the same 96 steps."}
plot(result, type = "posterior", segment = longest, step_range = c(1, 96))
```

The track and habitat raster come from the article's
[Figshare supplement](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34077912.v2).
The original GPS data are also available in the
[archive of Klappstein, Thomas and Michelot](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7872602).
